blocks.raw:
<Callout>

Feminist and postcolonial perspectives fundamentally challenge architecture's traditional canon, revealing how architectural discourse has been structured by patriarchal and colonial assumptions, and how spaces—domestic, institutional, public—reproduce and enforce gender and racial hierarchies. The LEA tests your understanding of how these perspectives expose architecture's political dimensions and how contemporary architects and theorists work toward more equitable, culturally-grounded, and socially-engaged practice.
</Callout>

blocks.raw: <Tip>Feminist architectural analysis hinges on this equation: **Domestic space = gendered space = political space**. Architectural history treated domestic design as minor/private; feminist analysis reveals it as fundamentally political—it enforces gender roles through spatial organization. This reframing (domesticity as political) is the entire conceptual move.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <Note>Dolores Hayden's *The Grand Domestic Revolution* (1981) is crucial because it shows feminism and architecture have *always* been intertwined. Women reformers imagined collective housing (shared kitchens, childcare centers) as *architectural solutions to patriarchal domesticity*—not as utopian fantasy but as practical contestation. This historical precedent proves that architectural feminism is not modern invention but recovery of suppressed tradition.</Note>

blocks.raw: <Warn>Feminist architectural critique is NOT "hire more women architects" (though visibility matters). The core claim is that **spaces encode power**—that patriarchal arrangements are *materialized* in building design. This requires looking at floor plans, spatial separation, circulation patterns, not just architect demographics. A femlea-designed building can still reproduce patriarchal spatial logic; gender inclusion without spatial criticism is insufficient.</Warn>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Universalizing Western Feminism. \"Feminism\" is not monolithic. Western feminist theory emphasizing individual autonomy may differ from feminist concerns in contexts where collective family structures are primary, or where anticolonial and feminist struggles are inseparable. Contemporary feminist scholarship is attentive to these differences.", "Separating Gender and Race/Postcolonial Analysis. Students sometimes analyze gender separately from race and imperialism. Intersectionality insists these are inseparable. Women of color, women in the Global South, and Indigenous women experience architecture through interlocking systems of domination.", "Assuming Postcolonial Architecture is Only Regional. Postcolonial architecture is not simply \"respect local traditions.\" Postcoloniality is a condition and analytical position regarding colonialism's ongoing effects. Contemporary Indian or Egyptian architecture engages global modernity while refusing complete Westernization.", "Missing Institutional and Pedagogical Dimensions. Decolonizing architecture requires not just different designs but transforming architectural education, professional structures, and canonization processes. Recognizing this systemic dimension is crucial to understanding feminist and postcolonial perspectives' full scope."]} />
